hints: Notice the shape from X to Y: thickness is uniform but width grows steadily with distance $x$, so cross-sectional area $A$ increases with $x$.
Recall $I = nAqv$ for a metal, so for the same current $I$ through every slice, $v$ must satisfy $v = I/(nAq)$ with $n$ and $q$ constant.
Since width varies linearly as $w_0 + kx$, $v$ varies as $1/(w_0 + kx)$, which decreases steeply at first then more slowly and never reaches zero.
walkthrough: End X at $x = 0$ is the narrow end and the Y end at $x = L$ is the wide end, with uniform thickness, so area $A = \text{thickness} \times \text{width}$ increases with $x$.
The conductor is in series with the cell, so the same current $I$ passes through every cross-section along $L$.
Use $I = nAqv$, where $n$ is electron number density and $q$ is electron charge, both constant for the metal. Rearranged, $v = I/(nqA)$ so $v$ is proportional to $1/A$.
Because width increases approximately linearly with $x$, write $A \propto (w_0 + kx)$, giving $v \propto 1/(w_0 + kx)$. This is largest at $x = 0$ and falls with $x$ but stays finite at $x = L$.
A $1/(w_0 + kx)$ dependence is a curved hyperbola, steep at first then flattening, not a straight line and not reaching zero.
Only the decreasing curved graph starting high at $x = 0$ and flattening toward $x = L$ matches this. This is option A.

A.explanation: Decreasing curve with $v$ largest at X and falling as $1/A$ where $A$ grows with $x$, matching $v = I/(nAq)$.

B.explanation: Increasing $v$ with $x$ is wrong because larger cross-sectional area at larger $x$ requires smaller $v$ for the same current $I$.

C.explanation: A straight line to zero is wrong because $v$ is inversely proportional to width, not linear, and $v$ cannot be zero while current flows.

D.explanation: Increasing from zero is wrong because $v$ is largest at the narrow end X and never zero in a current-carrying conductor.
